title: The yield strength of a body when its shape was set, by material, and how the materials mix (GEN.1158, physics/roundness.py)
note: This file is where measured strengths drop in. Every number here is a stand-in (registry rows RN1 to RN7, section 6.126 of the gap filling plan); a material gives either 'strength_pa' (a strength at the scale of a body, Pa) or 'round_radius_km' with 'reference_density_kg_m3' (the mean radius at which bodies of that material and density were seen to turn round; the strength that rounds a body at that size is worked out from it). 'same_as' gives a material the strength of another until it has its own. 'mixing', 'porosity', 'temperature' and 'rubble' each name a rule of physics/roundness.py (MIXING_RULES, POROSITY_RULES, TEMPERATURE_RULES, RUBBLE_RULES) and its numbers. A new rule is one function and one name; the engine's interface (ice fraction, metal fraction, porosity and a shape-set temperature in; strength, round radius, roundness ratio out) does not change. Values follow /mnt/project-files/reports/planetary-material-strength-2026-10-31.md, section 7 and section 11.

ice.label: water ice and the other ices of an icy moon, at the strength of ice near 160 K (the default when no shape-set temperature is given)
ice.source: Lineweaver and Norman 2010 (arXiv:1004.1091) fit of 0.4 to 3 MPa; equals the Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 creep strength of pure ice near 158 K at 1e-15 per second (strength research section 11a)

rock.label: silicate rock of an asteroid or rocky moon
rock.source: Lineweaver and Norman 2010 (arXiv:1004.1091) Fig. 2: Pallas 275 km and Vesta 265 km round, Juno 115 km not; confirmed three ways in strength research section 6 (range 4 to 30 MPa)

metal.label: iron and nickel metal
metal.source: Pohl and Britt 2020 iron meteorite lab yield 320 to 450 MPa and kamacite single crystal 134 MPa at 300 K, divided by 2 to 6 for inclusions and cracks (strength research section 5)

mixing.source: strength of ice with hard grains = ice strength x exp(2 x grain volume fraction), measured to 0.56 (Durham et al. 1992 as printed in Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 eq. 3); continued to 0.65 (random close packing, recalled) then geometric to the solids' strength at 1 (an extrapolation of the strength research)

porosity.source: off: Pohl and Britt 2020 find no clear strength trend with porosity in meteorites. 'exponential' (strength x exp(-b x porosity), b 4 to 7, a ceramics-based recalled placeholder, 'coefficient' here) is built and not used; it would make Proteus round; the b range is widened to 4 to 9 by meteorite-to-boulder comparisons (papers-vs-standins-2026-10-31.md section 5)

ice.source: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 (JGR 102:16293) Table 2, dislocation creep of pure ice I (grain size 0.6 to 1 mm); strain rate = A sigma^n exp(-E / RT); the weakest regime governs; the pressure term is dropped (small bodies); an upper bound at the lowest stresses. Rate 1e-15 per second is a tunable stand-in (strength research section 11a)

columns.label: Hirth and Kohlstedt 2003, dry dislocation creep (as printed in Korenaga and Karato 2008 Table 3)
Korenaga and Karato 2008 re-fit, dry dislocation creep

rock.source: Korenaga and Karato 2008 (JGR 113 B02403) Table 3, READ; dry olivine at 1e-15 per second: 29 to 39 MPa at 1100 K, 7 to 13 at 1200 K, 2 to 5 at 1300 K, 0.8 to 2 at 1400 K; never above the cold whole-body rock strength (which stands for the brittle Byerlee limit below about 900 K); pressure term dropped; Chu and Korenaga 2012 test the laws at geologic rates. Intact olivine crystal strength (10 GPa, Wallis 2020) is never used

rubble.source: friction angle 35 degrees (30 to 40 for geological material, Lambe and Whitman 1969, a soil mechanics textbook) with cohesion 44 to 210 Pa: Hirabayashi and Scheeres (arXiv 1411.5926, READ), Rozitis, MacLennan and Emery 2014 (Nature 512:174, READ) for 1950 DA 64 (+12, -20) Pa, Sanchez and Scheeres 2014 and Walsh 2018 (READ); hot_strength_pa is a rubble pile that took its shape hot, 2.5 MPa, the creep strength of dry olivine (the two columns of 'temperature.rock') at about 1330 K, range 1 to 4 MPa for 1250 to 1400 K (papers-vs-standins-2026-10-31.md section 2)

ice_types.note: The strength of each kind of ice as a ratio to the strength of ice Ih at the same shape-set temperature (GEN.1177, strength research sections 2b, 9, 11c and 14). physics/ice_types.py reads it and names a body's ice type; nothing in the roundness engine reads it yet. 'strength_ratio' multiplies the Ih strength; 'strength_pa' is an absolute strength at the scale of a body (the type is then not scaled by the Ih law); 'ratio_by_temperature_k' is a list of [temperature K, ratio] points, log-linear in the ratio, held at the end values beyond them.

ice_ih.label: water ice Ih, the ice of a body that stays under about 0.2 GPa
ice_ih.source: the reference: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 creep law (section 11a), the 'ice' material of this file

ice_ii.label: ice II, the cold phase from 0.2 to 0.6 GPa
ice_ii.source: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 Table 2 (READ), the strain rate A sigma^n exp(-(E + P V) / R T) of each phase at 1e-15 per second over the three-regime ice Ih law at the same temperature (reports/papers-vs-standins-2026-10-31.md section 1; the ratios of two dislocation laws, an upper bound at low stress because grain-size-sensitive creep is weaker there); phase pressure 400 MPa; 1.7 at 150 K, 0.9 to 1 at 180 K (the Ih regime change) and 5 to 6.5 from 200 to 250 K; the ratios move by 40 percent at most between 1e-14 and 1e-16 per second; held at the end values

ice_iii.label: ice III, the narrow wedge near 0.2 to 0.35 GPa and 240 to 256 K
ice_iii.source: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 Table 2 (READ), the strain rate A sigma^n exp(-(E + P V) / R T) of each phase at 1e-15 per second over the three-regime ice Ih law at the same temperature (reports/papers-vs-standins-2026-10-31.md section 1; the ratios of two dislocation laws, an upper bound at low stress because grain-size-sensitive creep is weaker there); phase pressure 300 MPa; 0.8 at 230 K and 0.45 at 250 K, the engine's wedge is 240 to 256 K; weaker than Ih by a factor of two, not by three decades (the earlier 0.001 read 'extremely weak' as near zero); below 230 K ice III is stronger than Ih but that is outside its field

ice_v.label: ice V, 0.35 to 0.63 GPa at 250 K and over
ice_v.source: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 Table 2 (READ), the strain rate A sigma^n exp(-(E + P V) / R T) of each phase at 1e-15 per second over the three-regime ice Ih law at the same temperature (reports/papers-vs-standins-2026-10-31.md section 1; the ratios of two dislocation laws, an upper bound at low stress because grain-size-sensitive creep is weaker there); phase pressure 500 MPa; about 8 at 230 to 250 K (the engine's field is 250 K and over), the points at 200 K and below are extrapolations of the law (the 100 at 150 K is left out, a far extrapolation); the 1997 paper notes the Poirier and Sotin ice V is about three orders more viscous than its own (unresolved), so the true strength may be higher still

ice_vi.label: ice VI, 0.63 to 2.2 GPa, and the value used for ice VII and ice X (no lab strength found)
ice_vi.source: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1997 Table 2 (READ), the strain rate A sigma^n exp(-(E + P V) / R T) of each phase at 1e-15 per second over the three-regime ice Ih law at the same temperature (reports/papers-vs-standins-2026-10-31.md section 1; the ratios of two dislocation laws, an upper bound at low stress because grain-size-sensitive creep is weaker there); phase pressure 1000 MPa; 5.5 at 150 K, 1.3 at 180 K and 4 to 5 at 200 to 230 K, held above (the law has no ice VI point at 250 K); strength research section 14: the ice VI constants stand for VII and X, which exist only inside bodies of over 1,000 km radius that are round by gravity

ch4_clathrate.label: methane clathrate hydrate (sI), water caging methane
ch4_clathrate.source: Durham, Kirby, Stern and Zhang 2003 (READ): 20 to 30 times stronger than ice Ih near 273 K and the contrast grows on cooling, a lower bound (partial dissociation during deformation); section 11c, 14: hydrate strength = 20 to 30 times ice at the same temperature and rate, do not extrapolate the n = 2.2 law below 260 K

co2_ice.label: solid carbon dioxide (dry ice)
co2_ice.source: Durham, Kirby and Stern 1999 (READ): markedly weaker than water ice, flow law A = 10^3.86 MPa^-n s^-1, n = 5.6, Q = 33 kJ/mol at 150 to 190 K; at 1e-15 per second the law gives 0.05 MPa at 150 K, 0.16 at 120 K and 0.5 at 100 K (my calculation, pressure term none), and the strength research section 9 asks for 0.1 to 0.5 MPa; 0.3 MPa is near 110 K

nh3_dihydrate.label: ammonia dihydrate, NH3 with two waters (and ammonia-water mixtures)
nh3_dihydrate.source: Durham and Kirby, NASA NTRS N92-10735 (READ): weaker than water ice near its 176 K melting point, more temperature sensitive, stronger below about 135 K; the three points are the interpolation of strength research section 14 (the 1993 constants of Durham, Kirby and Stern are not in hand)

phases.note: Which phase of water ice a body's centre holds, from its central pressure (and the shape-set temperature for the narrow wedges). Boundaries are the usual water phase diagram (recalled, row IT8); the lookup is a stand-in for bodies whose centre is over 0.2 GPa, which are nearly all round already.

composition.note: How the ice type of a body is named from its components (`small_body_composition` shares of the ice group). A hydrate is named when the cage-filling share of the ice is over the threshold; the ammonia type when ammonia is that share of the ice; otherwise the dominant ice by mass.
